details:
**"Daddy" and "a man in black with a Meinkampf look"**
Plath's most famous poem, written in 1962 and published in Ariel, is addressed to her father, Otto Plath, a German-born professor and bee expert who died when she was eight. Using Holocaust and Nazi imagery, the speaker casts her father as a Nazi and herself as a Jew. She calls him "a man in black with a Meinkampf look," a "ghastly statue with one gray toe / Big as a Frisco seal," and a teacher who stands "at the blackboard" with "a cleft in your chin instead of your foot."

**"You do not do, you do not do" and "you bastard, I'm through"**
The opening and closing lines of "Daddy." The father is a "black shoe / In which I have lived like a foot / For thirty years." The speaker says "Daddy, I have had to kill you. / You died before I had time," and the poem ends "There's a stake in your fat black heart / And the villagers never liked you... Daddy, daddy, you bastard, I'm through."

**"Every woman adores a Fascist"**
Another line from "Daddy," in which the speaker says she has "always been scared of you, / With your Luftwaffe, your gobbledygoo," and stammers "Ich, ich, ich, ich" when trying to speak German. She rejects the "snows of the Tyrol" and "the clear beer of Vienna" and recalls a Polish town "scraped flat by the roller / Of wars, wars, wars." The father figure merges with "the vampire who said he was you / And drank my blood for a year," widely read as her husband, Ted Hughes.

**"Lady Lazarus" and "I eat men like air"**
A 1962 poem in Ariel in which the speaker, like the biblical Lazarus, keeps returning from death. It opens "I have done it again. / One year in every ten / I manage it," and ends with a threat to "Herr God, Herr Lucifer": "Out of the ash / I rise with my red hair / And I eat men like air."

**"Dying / Is an art, like everything else"**
The most famous lines of "Lady Lazarus," which continue "I do it exceptionally well. / I do it so it feels like hell." The speaker, who is "only thirty" and "like the cat" has "nine times to die," calls this suicide attempt "Number Three. / What a trash / To annihilate each decade." She taunts "Peel off the napkin / O my enemy. / Do I terrify?" and uses Holocaust images such as "a cake of soap, / A wedding ring, / A gold filling."

**Ariel**
Plath's posthumous 1965 collection, edited by Ted Hughes, which contains "Daddy," "Lady Lazarus," "Tulips," and "Morning Song." Its title poem, named for a horse she rode, begins "Stasis in darkness. / Then the substanceless blue" and calls the horse "God's lioness." The speaker unpeels "dead hands, dead stringencies," becomes "the arrow, / The dew that flies," and ends "at one with the drive / Into the red / Eye, the cauldron of morning."

**The Bell Jar and Esther Greenwood**
Plath's only novel (1963), first published under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas about a month before her death. Esther Greenwood, a college student on a summer internship at Ladies' Day magazine in New York, befriends Doreen and pictures her life as a fig tree whose branching choices wither as she fails to pick one. She sinks into depression, receives botched electroshock therapy from Dr. Gordon, attempts suicide, and recovers under Dr. Nolan at a private hospital paid for by the novelist Philomena Guinea.

**Ted Hughes and Plath's 1963 suicide**
Plath married the English poet Ted Hughes in 1956, and his first collection, The Hawk in the Rain, is dedicated to her. They separated in 1962 after his affair, and in February 1963 she killed herself by putting her head in a gas oven in London. Hughes's 1998 collection Birthday Letters, a set of poems addressed to her, includes "The Blue Flannel Suit."

**"Mad Girl's Love Song"**
An early villanelle that repeats "I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead" and the parenthetical refrain "(I think I made you up inside my head.)" The speaker imagines "the stars go waltzing out in blue and red" and wishes "I should have loved a thunderbird instead."

**"The Munich Mannequins"**
A late poem opening "Perfection is terrible, it cannot have children." It describes the "morgue between Paris and Rome," the shop-window mannequins "naked and bald in their furs, / Orange lollies on silver sticks," and ends "The snow has no voice."

**"Tulips"**
A 1961 poem written after Plath was hospitalized for surgery. The speaker wants to be blank and at peace: "I am nobody; I have nothing to do with explosions," having given "my history to the anesthetist and my body to surgeons." The nurses pass "the way gulls pass inland in their white caps," and the vivid red tulips seem to "eat my oxygen" and force her back to life.

**"The Colossus"**
The title poem of Plath's first collection (1960), in which the speaker tries to piece together a huge ruined statue representing her dead father. She calls him "pithy and historical as the Roman Forum" and says "A blue sky out of the Oresteia / Arches above us."

**"The Applicant"**
A satirical poem in which a salesman pitches a wife to a man as if she were a product. She will "bring teacups," "do whatever you tell it," sew, and cook, and the poem ends "Will you marry it, marry it, marry it."

**"Morning Song"**
The poem opening Ariel, about the birth of her daughter, which begins "Love set you going like a fat gold watch." It ends with the baby's "clear vowels" that "rise like balloons."

**"Mirror"**
A poem spoken by a mirror that is "silver and exact" and has "no preconceptions," and that later becomes a lake. A woman bends over it every day, and it ends: "In me she has drowned a young girl, and in me an old woman / Rises toward her day after day, like a terrible fish."
